v-urbs: Urbs, urbis is a third-declension feminine noun. Livy's history of Rome is called Ab urbe conditā, 'from the founding of the city', and Romans counted years that way too (AUC).
v-via: Via, viae is first declension. Roman roads were built in layers of stone and gravel, with milestones (mīliāria) every Roman mile, about 1,480 m. Spartacus' followers were crucified along the Via Appia in 71 BC.
g-sum-est: Sum, es, est is irregular but the most common verb in Latin. Est connects two nominatives: Rōma (subject) and urbs (complement). The bronze Capitoline Wolf, in Rome's Capitoline Museums, is the city's symbol.
g-1decl-nom: First-declension nouns end in -a in the nominative singular and -ae in the plural. A few are masculine because of their meaning, like nauta, 'sailor', and agricola, 'farmer'.
x-map-roma: Rome grew up on hills beside the Tiber, which made them easy to defend. The Capitoline held the temple of Jupiter; the Forum lay in the marshy valley below, drained by the Cloaca Maxima.
v-pater: Pater, patris and māter, mātris are third declension. In law a father could even sell or put to death his children, though this was rare in practice. English 'patrician' comes from patrēs, the senators.
v-filius: Fīlius, fīliī is second declension; its vocative is fīlī. Roman daughters usually had only the family name in feminine form, so Cicero's daughter was simply Tullia.
g-acc: The accusative marks the direct object: the person or thing that receives the action. Pater fīlium amat and Fīlium pater amat mean the same, while Fīlius patrem amat reverses it.
g-2decl: Second-declension nouns end in -us (masculine) or -um (neuter) in the nominative. Neuter plurals end in -a: dōnum, dōna. Rome's enslaved population was huge, perhaps 10–20% of Italy under Augustus.
d-familia: Domus, 'house', is irregular, with locative domī, 'at home'. A rich Roman's domus had an atrium with an opening in the roof and a pool below to catch rain.
l-bulla: Bulla means 'bubble', from its round shape; rich families' bullae were gold, poorer ones leather. Girls wore a lunula, a crescent amulet, until marriage.
x-whosays-cornelia: Cornelia (c. 190–100 BC) was praised by Roman writers for her learning and her letters. A statue of her stood in Rome with the inscription 'Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi'.
v-miles: Mīles, mīlitis is third declension: find the stem from the genitive. Legionaries were citizens and carried their own kit on a pole, earning the nickname 'Marius' mules'.
v-castra: Castra is plural in form but means one camp; its singular castrum meant a fort. Camps were laid out on a fixed grid with two main streets, a pattern still visible in towns like Chester.
g-1conj: First-conjugation verbs have -ā- in their stem, like amāre and ambulāre. The personal endings -ō, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt show who is acting, so Latin rarely needs a pronoun.
g-2conj: Second-conjugation verbs have -ē- in their stem: vidēre, monēre. The endings are the same as the first conjugation: videt, vident. The centurion was the backbone of the legion's discipline.
i-vindolanda: More than 1,000 ink-written wooden tablets have been found at Vindolanda, near Hadrian's Wall, since 1973. They are now in the British Museum and include letters, lists and requests for beer and socks.
l-pila: Each legionary carried one or two pīla, about 2 m long, and threw them from about 15–20 m. A pilum stuck in a shield made it too heavy to use, forcing the enemy to drop it.
x-parse-signum: The Twentieth Legion probably won the title Valeria Victrix in the defeat of Boudica in AD 60–61. It was based at Chester (Deva) for about two centuries.
v-res-publica: Rēs is fifth declension, and pūblica agrees with it as an adjective. Romans dated the Republic from the expulsion of the kings in 509 BC to Augustus' rule from 27 BC.
v-senatus: Senātus is fourth declension, with genitive senātūs. Under the Republic the Senate had about 300 members, later 600 and then 900 under Caesar. Roman years were named after the two consuls, for example 'when Cicero and Antonius were consuls'.
g-gen: The genitive shows possession or connection, usually translated with 'of'. First declension -ae, second -ī, third -is. The temple of Saturn's surviving columns are from a 4th-century AD rebuilding.
g-dat: The dative marks the indirect object, the person to or for whom something is done; here Caesarī, 'to Caesar'. Caesar was killed on 15 March 44 BC.
g-adj: First- and second-declension adjectives like bonus, bona, bonum have three endings, one for each gender. The adjective usually follows its noun in Latin.
l-toga: The toga was a large semicircle of wool, about 5–6 m across, wrapped around the body. Boys wore the purple-bordered toga praetexta until they came of age; magistrates wore it too.
d-dico: The four principal parts give you every form of the verb: present, infinitive, perfect, supine. Benedictus, 'blessed', and maledictus, 'cursed', literally mean 'well-spoken' and 'badly-spoken'.
v-deus: Deus is second declension; its vocative is deus or dīve. Romans made offerings to the gods to keep the pāx deōrum, 'the peace of the gods', on which the state's success depended.
v-templum: Most Roman temples stood on a high podium with steps only at the front. Inside, the cella housed the cult statue; sacrifices took place at an altar outside.
g-3decl: Third-declension nouns have many nominatives but regular stems: rēx, rēg-; lēx, lēg-; pāx, pāc-. Learn the genitive with each noun. The word pāx gives English 'peace' and 'pacify'.
g-abl-prep: The ablative shows place, means and separation and is used after prepositions like in, cum, ex, ab and dē. The temple of Vesta held the sacred hearth fire of the Roman state.
i-pantheon-parse: L·F is Lūciī fīlius, 'son of Lucius'; COS is cōnsul. Romans used abbreviations constantly in inscriptions, because carving letters in stone was slow and costly.
l-lares: The Lares were protective spirits of the household and the crossroads; the Penates guarded the food store. Families made offerings to them on special days such as births and marriages.
v-imperator: Imperātor comes from imperāre, 'to command'. The Prima Porta statue shows Augustus as a general addressing his troops, his breastplate celebrating the return of standards from Parthia.
g-perf-rg: The perfect tense describes completed past actions: gessī, 'I waged'. Most perfect forms end in -ī in the first person and -it in the third person.
g-impf: The imperfect describes repeated or ongoing past action: aedificābant, 'they used to build'. Augustus' building programme included the Forum of Augustus with the temple of Mars Ultor, dedicated in 2 BC.
g-possum: Possum is a compound of pot- (able) and sum: pos-sum, pot-es, pot-est. Its infinitive is posse, and the English word 'possible' comes from it.
i-coin-divi-f: After Julius Caesar was declared a god in 42 BC, Octavian could call himself 'son of a god'. Coins were the mass media of the ancient world, carrying the ruler's image and message everywhere.
l-denarius: The silver denarius was introduced around 211 BC, during the Second Punic War. Over the empire its silver content dropped sharply, especially in the 3rd century AD.
x-timeline-emp: Augustus ruled from 27 BC to AD 14. The empire in the west ended in 476, when Romulus Augustulus was deposed; the eastern empire lasted until 1453.
v-amo: Amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum: the four principal parts. Words like 'amiable', 'amateur' (one who loves something) and 'amorous' come from this family.
g-imperative: Carpe is the singular imperative of carpere, 'to pluck'. Horace's Odes 1.11 is only eight lines long; the whole line is carpe diem, quam minimum crēdula posterō.
g-future: First- and second-conjugation verbs form the future with -bō, -bis, -bit (amābō); third and fourth use -am, -ēs, -et (regam). Nōn omnis moriar means 'I shall not wholly die'.
g-pronoun: Latin verbs already show the person, so ego and tū are used mainly for emphasis or contrast. The dative mihi, 'to me', appears in many famous lines, such as Mūsa, mihi causās memorā.
v-tempus: Tempus, temporis is a third-declension neuter noun, so its nominative and accusative are the same. Romans divided daylight into twelve hours, which were longer in summer than in winter.
x-meter: Each hexameter has six feet, made of long and short syllables in patterns of dactyls (long-short-short) and spondees (long-long). Reading aloud is the best way to hear the rhythm.
v-animus: Animus is the thinking, feeling mind; anima is the breath of life or the soul. Seneca and Marcus Aurelius taught that only the animus is truly in our control.
g-infinitive: The infinitive is the 'to' form of the verb: vīvere, 'to live'; mīlitāre, 'to serve as a soldier'. Here both act as nouns joined by est. The line is from Letter 96.
g-ind-stat: After verbs of saying and thinking, Latin uses an accusative and infinitive: Rōmulum … condidisse. Livy tells the founding story in Book 1 of his history, with the traditional date of 753 BC.
d-video: Videō, vidēre, vīdī, vīsum gives words from both stems: 'video' from vid-, 'vision', 'visit' and 'visual' from vīs-. Caesar's vēnī, vīdī, vīcī uses the perfect, vīdī.
x-greek-flag: Marcus Aurelius (emperor 161–180) wrote his private notes during campaigns on the Danube. Educated Romans studied Greek from childhood and often travelled to Athens or Rhodes to complete their education.
l-schola: Schola comes from the Greek word scholē, 'leisure', because study was what free time was for. Pupils learned by copying, reciting and memorising, and teachers were known for beating them.
g-passive: In the perfect passive, Latin uses the participle plus sum: capta est, 'was captured'. Augustine's City of God, written 413–426, argued that Christianity was not to blame for Rome's fall.
i-chirho: The Chi-Rho combines the first two Greek letters of Christ's name, X (chi) and P (rho). Alpha and Omega, first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, mean 'the beginning and the end'.
v-rex: Rēx, rēgis is third declension, from the same root as regere, 'to rule'. Theodoric (ruled 493–526) kept Roman law and the Senate working and employed Roman scholars such as Boethius and Cassiodorus.
x-vulgate: Pope Damasus commissioned Jerome to revise the Latin Gospels around 382. Jerome went on to translate much of the Old Testament from Hebrew. Vulgāta means 'commonly used'.
d-crux: Crux, crucis is third declension. Christians at first avoided showing the cross; it became a common Christian symbol only after crucifixion had ended in the 4th century.
l-annona: Annōna comes from annus, 'year', the year's harvest; it was also the name of the official grain supply. About 200,000 citizens received free grain under Augustus. Egypt and North Africa supplied much of it.
g-relative: The relative pronoun quī, quae, quod agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but takes its case from its own clause. Here quī refers to Pater and is the subject of es.
v-liber: Liber originally meant the inner bark of a tree, an early writing material. Legō, 'I read', also means 'I gather', because reading is gathering words.
l-monasterium: Monasterium comes from the Greek monos, 'alone'. The Plan of Saint Gall (c. 820) is a drawing of an ideal monastery with church, library, school, kitchens, gardens and workshops.
i-karolus: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's, Rome, on Christmas Day 800. His coin reform introduced the silver penny (denarius) used across Europe for centuries.
x-colophon: Incipit means 'it begins' and explicit is short for explicitus est, 'it has been unrolled', from ancient scrolls. Colophons can record the scribe's name, the date and the place a book was made.
x-map-medieval: Monasteries such as Lindisfarne, founded 635, and Iona copied and preserved Latin texts. Charlemagne's court at Aachen gathered scholars like Alcuin, and Carolingian scribes copied many classical works that survive only through them.
d-scribo: Scrībō, scrībere, scrīpsī, scrīptum is a third-conjugation verb. Medieval scribes wrote on parchment made from animal skin, using quills and ink made from oak galls.
